1. Straight-line regression¶

  • Regression is one of the most widely used statistical models.
  • Suppose we have a sample $(X_1,Y_1)$, $(X_2,Y_2)$, ... , $(X_N,Y_N)$ of two random variables. We would like to explain (or predict) the Y-values based on the X-values. In this case, we say Y is the "response" variable and X is the "explanatory" or "predictor" variable.

  • Line regression model:

    $Y_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n + \eps_n;\quad \text{ for } n = 1,2,\dots, N,$

    where $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ are unknown parameters (or coefficients) and $\eps_1$, ... , $\eps_N$ are random variables representing error.

  • The following assumptions are usually made for a line regression model $\newcommand{\Var}{\operatorname{Var}}$ $\newcommand{\sig}{\sigma}$ $\newcommand{\Eb}{\mathbb{E}}$

    1. $\Eb(\eps_i)=0$

    2. $\eps_1,\ldots, \eps_N$ are independent

    3. $\Var(\eps_n)=\sig_\eps^2$, for all $n$

    4. $\eps_n$ are normally distributed

  • The conditions above are summarized by the notation $~\eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}N(0,\sig_\eps^2)$
  • Here, i.i.d. stands for independent and identically distributed
  • We may also say that $\{\eps_n\}_{n=1}^N$ is a normal (or Gaussian) white noise

1.1 Least-squares (LS) estimation of the coefficients¶

  • Our first goal is to "fit" the line regression model (to the sample $\{(X_n,Y_n)\}_{n=1}^N$). That is, to find "good estimates" of the unknown coefficients $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$

  • There are three main approaches to fit statistical models:

    a. Least-squares (LS) estimation

    b. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)

    c. Bayesian estimation

  • We use the simplest method, namely LS. In this method, the estimate of the parameter are the minimizers of the the sum of the squared errors

    $f(b_0, b_1) = \sum_{n=1}^N \Big[Y_n - (b_0 + b_1 X_n)\Big]^2$

  • We denote the estimate of parameters $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$ by $\betah_0$ and $\betah_1$, respectively. Then, the estimates are given by

    $(\betah_0, \betah_1) = \underset{b_0, b_1}{\arg\min}\; f(b_0, b_1)$

  • The function $f(b_0,b_1)$ is shown to be a convex function. Therefore, its global minimizer $(\betah_0, \betah_1)$ is the uniques solution of the system of equation
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial b_0}(\betah_0, \betah_1) = 0\\ \displaystyle\frac{\partial f}{\partial b_1}(\betah_0, \betah_1) = 0 \end{cases} \end{align*}
\begin{align*} \Longrightarrow\quad \begin{cases} \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^N Y_n - N\,\betah_0 - \betah_1 \sum_{n=1}^N X_n = 0\\ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^N X_n Y_n - \betah_0\,\sum_{n=1}^N X_n - \betah_1\, \sum_{n=1}^N X_n^2=0 \end{cases} \end{align*}

  • Solving this system of linear equations yields $\newcommand{\Xb}{\bar{X}}\newcommand{\Yb}{\bar{Y}}$

    $\betah_1 = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N (Y_n - \Yb)(X_n-\Xb)}{\sum_{n=1}^N (X_n-\Xb)^2},\quad\text{ and }\quad\betah_0 = \Yb - \betah_1 \Xb$

    where we have defined $\Xb = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N X_n}{N}$ and $\Yb = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N Y_n}{N}$

  • The formulas for $\betah_1$ is usually expressed in the following form

    $\displaystyle \betah_1 = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N Y_n(X_n-\Xb)}{\sum_{n=1}^N (X_n-\Xb)^2} = \frac{S_{XY}}{S_X^2}$

  • Here, the sample variance $S_X^2$ and sample covariance $S_{XY}$ are

    $\displaystyle S^2_X = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N (X_n-\Xb)^2}{N-1}$, and $\displaystyle S_{XY} = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N (Y_n - \Yb)(X_n-\Xb)}{N-1}$

  • The least square line is given by $\newcommand{\Yh}{\hat{Y}}$
\begin{align*} \Yh = \betah_0 + \betah_1 X = \Yb + \betah_1 (X-\Xb) = \Yb + \frac{S_{XY}}{S_X^2}(X-\Xb) \end{align*}
  • $\Yh_n = \betah_0 + \betah_1 X_n$ is called the "fitted value" of $Y$ (at $X_n$)$\newcommand{\epsh}{\hat{\eps}}$
  • $\epsh_n = Y_n - \Yh_n$, $n=1,\ldots,N$, are called the "residuals". They are estimates of the error $\eps_n = Y_n - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_n$.
  • Note the difference between residuals and errors!
  • Let us see how to fit a line regression in R.
  • We want to see if there is a linear relationship between government interest rate and corporate interest rate.
  • Let us obtain historical 10-year Treasury constant maturity rate (symbol DGS10) and Moody's seasoned corporate AAA yields (symbol AAA), both of which are available from FRED.

  • With the sample $\{(\text{WAAA}_n, \text{DGS10}_n)\}_{n=1}^{881}$ at hand, let us fit the line regression

    $\Delta \text{WAAA}_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \Delta \text{DGS10}_n + \eps_n$

  • Here, $\Delta \text{WAAA}_n= \text{WAAA}_n - \text{WAAA}_{n-1}$ is the weekly corporate rate change. Similarly, $\Delta \text{DGS10}_n = \text{DGS10}_n - \text{DGS10}_{n-1}$ is the weekly treasury rate change.
In [6]:
# Calculating the differences
AAA_dif = diff(as.vector(dat[,"WAAA"]))
DGS10_dif = diff(as.vector(dat[,"DGS10"]))
  • Next, we fit the line regression model, using the R function lm(), and output the summary.
  • The fitted line is
\begin{align*} \Delta \text{WAAA}_n = -0.000669 + 0.3232680\, \Delta \text{DGS10}_n + \eps_n \end{align*}

# Fitting a linear model
fit1 <- lm(AAA_dif ~ DGS10_dif)
summary(fit1)

2. The variance of $\betah_1$¶

  • Consider the line regression model:

    $Y_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n + \eps_n;\quad \text{ for } n = 1,2,\dots, N,$

    $~\eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim}N(0,\sig_\eps^2)$

  • We showed that the LS estimates of the parameters are

    $\betah_1 = \sum_{n=1}^N\left(\frac{(X_n-\Xb)}{\sum_{n'=1}^N (X_{n'}-\Xb)^2}\right)Y_n = \frac{S_{XY}}{S_X^2},\quad\text{ and }\quad\betah_0 = \Yb - \betah_1 \Xb$

    where we have defined the sample averages $\Xb = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N X_n}{N}$ and $\Yb = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N Y_n}{N}$, the sample variance $S^2_X := \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N (X_n-\Xb)^2}{N-1}$, and the sample covariance $S_{XY} = \frac{\sum_{n=1}^N (Y_n - \Yb)(X_n-\Xb)}{N-1}$

  • Q: How reliable are these estimates? How much error do they contain?
  • Variance of an estimator is a good indicator of its error
  • We can write $\betah_1 := \sum_{n=1}^N w_n Y_n$, where
\begin{align*} w_n:=\frac{X_n-\Xb}{\sum_{n'=1}^N(X_{n'}-\Xb)^2} \end{align*}
  • Note that
\begin{align*} \sum_{n=1}^N w_n^2 = \sum_{n=1}^N\left(\frac{X_n-\Xb}{\sum_{n'=1}^N (X_{n'}-\Xb)^2}\right)^2= \frac{1}{\sum_{n'=1}^N(X_{n'}-\Xb)^2} = \frac{1}{(N-1)S_X^2} \end{align*}
  • We then have:
\begin{align*} \Var\left(\betah_1|X_1,\dots,X_N\right) &= \Var\left(\sum_{n=1}^N w_n Y_n|X_1,\dots,X_N\right)\\ &=\sum_{n=1}^N w_n^2 \Var\left(Y_n|X_1,\dots,X_N\right) \quad\text{($Y_n$-s are uncorrelated | $X_n$-s)}\\ &=\sum_{n=1}^n w_n^2 \Var\left(\beta_0+\beta_1 X_n + \eps_n |X_1,\dots,X_N\right)\\ &=\sum_{n=1}^n w_n^2 \Var(\eps_n|X_1,\dots,X_N)\\ &=\sigma_\eps^2\sum_{n=1}^{N} w_n^2 = \frac{\sig_\eps^2}{(N-1)S_X^2} \end{align*}
  • $\Var\left(\betah_1|X_1,\dots,X_n\right) = \frac{\sig_\eps^2}{(N-1)S_X^2}$
  • Thus, the variance of $\betah_1$ is smaller (in other words, $\betah_1$ is a better estimator) if:
    • $\sig_\eps^2$ is smaller (less noise),
    • $N$ is larger (bigger sample), or
    • $S_X^2$ is larger (more variation in the observed predictor values).

  • Using a similar argument, we can find the variance of $\betah_0$

  • Many statistical softwares (such as R) calculate the variance of estimates (or their standard deviation)

  • Consider the earlier example involving 10-year Treasury constant maturity rate (symbol DGS10) and Moody's seasoned corporate AAA yields (symbol WAAA), both of which are available from FRED

3. Multiple linear regression¶

  • In a multiple regression model, we have several predictors $X_1$, $X_2$, ... , $X_p$

  • We only have one response variable $Y$, however

    Regression models with many response variable are called multivariate

  • We are given the following sample of N observations:

    1st observation: $X_{1,1}, \dots, X_{1,p}$, and $Y_1$

    2nd observation: $X_{2,1}, \dots, X_{2,p}$, and $Y_2$

    $\vdots$

    N-th observation: $X_{N,1}, \dots, X_{N,p}$, and $Y_N$

  • The multiple linear regression model assumes that

    $Y_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{n,1} + \dots + \beta_p X_{n,p} + \eps_n;\quad n\in\{1,\dots,N\},$

    where $\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p$ are unknown parameters and $\eps_n\overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} N(0,\sig_\eps^2)$

  • The LS estimators of $\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p$, denoted by $\betah_0,\dots,\betah_p$, are the minimizers of the following optimization problem

    $\displaystyle\betah_0,\dots,\betah_p = \underset{\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p\in\Rb}{\arg\min}\, f(\beta_0,\dots,\beta_p)$

    where the sum of squares error function $f$ is given by

    $\displaystyle f(b_0,\dots,b_p) := \sum_{n=1}^N \left(Y_n - b_0 - b_1 X_{n,1} - \dots - b_p X_{n,p}\right)^2$

  • Using matrix notations simplifies the formulas. The N equations of the multiple linear regression model can be written in the matrix form
\begin{align*} \begin{pmatrix} Y_1\\ \vdots\\ Y_N \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_{1,1} & \dots & X_{1,p}\\ \vdots\\ 1 & X_{N,1} & \dots & X_{N,p}\\ \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0\\ \vdots\\ \beta_p \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \eps_1\\ \vdots\\ \eps_N \end{pmatrix} \end{align*}
  • Let us define
\begin{align*} \Yv:= \begin{pmatrix} Y_1\\ \vdots\\ Y_N \end{pmatrix}, \quad \Xv:= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & X_{1,1} & \dots & X_{1,p}\\ \vdots\\ 1 & X_{N,1} & \dots & X_{N,p}\\ \end{pmatrix}, \quad \betav:= \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0\\ \vdots\\ \beta_p \end{pmatrix}, \quad\text{and}\quad\epsv:= \begin{pmatrix} \eps_1\\ \vdots\\ \eps_N \end{pmatrix}, \end{align*}
  • Then, the multiple linear regression model becomes: $\Yv = \Xv\,\betav + \epsv$
  • The sum of squared error function $f$ can be written in matrix form, as follows
\begin{align*} &f(\bv) = \|\Yv - \Xv\bv\|^2 \\ &=(\Yv - \Xv\bv)^\top(\Yv - \Xv\bv) = (\bv^\top\Xv^\top - \Yv^\top)(\Xv\bv - \Yv)\\ &= \bv^\top \Xv^\top \Xv \bv - 2 \Yv^\top \Xv \bv + \Yv\Yv^\top \end{align*}
\begin{align*} &= \bv^\top \Xv^\top \Xv\, \underbrace{(\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1} \Xv^\top \Xv}\, \bv - 2 \Yv^\top \Xv \underbrace{(\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1} \Xv^\top \Xv}\,\bv + \underbrace{\Yv^\top \Xv (\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1} \Xv^\top \Yv}\\ &\qquad\underbrace{- \Yv^\top \Xv (\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1} \Xv^\top \Yv} +\Yv\Yv^\top\\ &= \left(\Xv^\top \Xv\, \bv - \Xv^\top \Yv\right)^\top (\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1} \left(\Xv^\top \Xv\, \bv- \Xv^\top \Yv\right) - \Yv^\top \Xv (\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1} \Xv^\top \Yv +\Yv\Yv^\top \end{align*}
  • Here, we assumed that the matrix $\Xv^\top \Xv$ is invertible. This assumption can be relaxed by using the pseudoinverse of $\Xv^\top \Xv$
  • Since $\Xv^\top \Xv$ is positive definite, so is the matrix $(\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1}$. Therefore, for all vectors $\bv$,
\begin{align*} \left(\Xv^\top \Xv\, \bv - \Xv^\top \Yv\right)^\top (\Xv^\top \Xv)^{-1} \left(\Xv^\top \Xv\, \bv - \Xv^\top \Yv\right)\ge 0 \end{align*}

  • From the expression for $f(\bv)$, it then follows that the least square estimate $\betavh$ should satisfy

    $\Xv^\top \Xv\, \betavh - \Xv^\top \Yv = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \betavh = (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}\Xv^\top \Yv$

  • This is the formula for the LS estimators of the multiple linear regression model
  • The n-th fitted value is
\begin{align*} \Yh_n = \betah_0 + \betah_1 X_{n,1} + \dots + \betah_p X_{n,p} \end{align*}
  • Define the vector of fitted values as follows $\Yvh:=\begin{pmatrix}\Yh_1\\\vdots\\\Yh_N\end{pmatrix}$
  • Then,
\begin{align*} \Yvh = \Xv \, \betavh = \Xv\, (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}\Xv^\top \Yv =: H\,\Yv \end{align*}
  • Here, the matrix $H := \Xv\, (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}\Xv^\top$ is called the "hat matrix" (since it transforms $\Yv$ into $\Yvh$)
  • Note that the hat matrix only depends on the values of the predictors $\Xv$
  • We can also calculate the variances (and covariances) of $\betavh$
\begin{align*} \Cov\left(\betavh\middle|\Xv\right) &= \Cov\left((\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}\Xv^\top \Yv\middle|\Xv\right)\\ &= (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}\Xv^\top\, \Cov\left( \Yv|X\right) \, \Xv (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}\\ &= (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}\Xv^\top\, \left(\sig_\eps^2\, \Iv\right) \, \Xv (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1} =\sig_\eps^2 (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1} \end{align*}
  • Here, $\Iv$ is the identity matrix

  • Thus, the variance of $\betah_k$ is the $k$-th diagonal element of $\sig_\eps^2 (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}$

    and the covariance of $\betah_k$ and $\betah_\ell$ is the $k\ell$ element of $\sig_\eps^2 (\Xv^\top\Xv)^{-1}$

  • The n-th residual is
\begin{align*} \epsh_n = Y_n - \Yh_n = Y_n - \betah_0 - \betah_1 X_{n,1} - \dots - \betah_p X_{n,p} \end{align*}
  • It estimates the error $\eps_n$
  • An "unbiased estimator" for $\sig_\eps^2$ is $\displaystyle\sigh_\eps^2 := \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^N \epsh_n^2}{N-1-p}$

Definition: A random variable $X$ is an unbiased estimator of the parameter $p$ if $\Eb(X)=p$

  • Let us fit a multiple linear regression model in R

4. Review of hypothesis testing¶

  • Next, we briefly go over statistical inference (hypothesis testing)
  • See Appendix A.18 of the textbook for more information
  • Statistical hypothesis testing is a framework by which one uses data to decide if a statement, called the "null hypothesis" and denoted by $H_0$, is true or not
  • The negation of the null hypothesis is called the "alternative hypothesis" and is denoted by $H_1$

Example:

  • We want to test if a random variable $Y$ has a linear dependence on another random variable $X$
  • we draw a sample $(X_1,Y_1), \dots, (X_N, Y_N)$ and consider the regression model $Y_n = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_n + \eps_n$
  • To test for linear dependence, we consider the null hypothesis of $\beta_1=0$ versus the alternative hypothesis $\beta_1\ne0$
  • This test is usually represented as follows
\begin{align*} \begin{cases} H_0: \beta_1=0,\\ H_1: \beta_1\ne0. \end{cases} \end{align*}
  • There are two approaches to conduct statistical tests: using test statistics or using p-values
  • A test statistic is an appropriate random variable that depends on the sample of observations. The choice of the test statistic depends on the type of test under consideration
  • "Rejection region" is a range of possible values of the test statistic
  • If the test statistic falls inside the rejection region, we reject $H_0$. Otherwise, we accept $H_0$

  • The rejection region is chosen to control the probability of the "type I error" of the test.

    Type I error: rejecting $H_0$ when it is true

  • The "significance level" (or simply the level) of a test is the probability of its type I error, that is
\begin{align*} \text{significance level} = \Pb\left(\text{test statistic in the rejection region}|H_0\right) \end{align*}

Example:

  • For the previous test, one suitable test statistic is $\displaystyle T = \frac{\betah_1}{\sqrt{\sigh_{\beta_1}^2}}$

    where $\displaystyle\sigh_{\beta_1}^2 = \frac{\sigh_\eps^2}{(N-1)S_X^2}$

  • It can be shown that if $H_0: \beta_1=0$ is correct, then T has a t-distribution with $N-p-1$ degrees of freedom
  • The rejection region for this test is $(-\infty, -x)\cup(x,+\infty)$, where the value of $x$ determines the significance level of the test

  • In particular, let $\al$ be the significance level. Then, by the symmetry of the t-distribution, we have

    $\displaystyle\al = \Pb\left(|T|>x\right) \Longrightarrow \Pb\left(T<-x\right)=\frac{\al}{2}$

  • In other words, $-x$ is $q_{\frac{\al}{2}}$, the $\frac{\al}{2}$-th quantile of the t-distribution with $N-p-1$ degree of freedom
  • Thus, the rejection region for a significance level of $\al$ is $(-\infty, q_{\frac{\al}{2}})\cup(-q_{\frac{\al}{2}},+\infty)$
  • Note that we need to find a new rejection region if we change the significance level, this is inconvenient
  • By using p-values, we can conduct statistical test for any level
  • The p-value corresponding to an observed value of a test statistic is the smallest significance level under which $H_0$ is rejected, assuming that $H_0$ is actually true
  • Intuitively, p-value measures the likelihood of $H_0$ given the observed value of the test statistic
  • P-values near zero indicates that the value of the test statistic is in favor of $H_1$. P-values near one are in favor of the $H_0$
  • To use p-value for conducting a test, simply compare it with the significance level $\al$. If p-value $\le \al$, then reject $H_0$. If p-value $> \al$ then accept $H_0$
  • The advantage of using p-values, instead of the test statistic and rejection region, is that one can repeat a test with different significance level without doing extra calculation for obtaining the rejection region

Example: In the previous example, the p-value for an observed value $t$ of the test statistic $T$ is

$\text{p-value}(t) = \Pb\left(|T|\ge t| H_0\right) = 2 \Pb\big(T<-|t|\,\big|\,H_0\big)$

4.1. Basic statistics and t-test for regression models¶

  • R reports 3 statistics for each estimate of the regression coefficients $\betah_0, \dots, \betah_p$:

    1. The standard error (SE) - An estimation of the standard deviation of $\betah_i$, indicates the precision of the estimator

    2. t-value - the t-test statistic for the null hypothesis $H_0: \beta_i=0$

    3. p-value corresponding to observed value of the t-test statistic

  • Note that significance of any $\betah_i$ (i.e. rejecting the hypothesis $H_0: \beta_i=0$) only indicates a linear relationship between that predictor and the test statistic
  • Regardless of the result of the test, there may be still non-linear relationships that should be investigated by other models
  • If a coefficient is insignificant, it only means that the corresponding predictor does not add more predictive power to the information already included in the of other predictors. In other words, the insignificant predictor may well be significant in a model that only includes it
